name: Rayburn murder cryptogram
date: cryptogram surfaced 2004-06 (killings themselves earlier; exact date of the cryptogram's writing not established in the source)
ciphertext_pending: No transcription of the roughly 80 characters exists in the post text or its comment thread (sources/schmeh/posts/43-rayburn.txt, read in full this pass) -- only one embedded image, files/2013/12/Rayburn-Cryptogram.jpg. A transcription pass from the image is the whole of cheap test 1.
alphabet: keyboard characters (letters upper- and lowercase, plus other keyboard symbols per Schmeh); every character is either underlined or crossed out -- a two-state marking on every symbol, distinct from ordinary substitution-cipher ciphertexts

constraints.marking: all characters underlined or crossed out (a binary annotation per symbol)
constraints.layout: the central part of the cryptogram is left-aligned, suggesting (per Schmeh) the author wrote left to right
constraints.frequency_analysis_caveat: Schmeh: 'A frequency analysis is obviously useless, as most characters appear only once' -- consistent with either a high-homophone cipher or, per Schmeh's own alternative reading, not a cipher of running text at all
constraints.diagram_hypothesis: Schmeh's own stated impression: 'looks like a diagram showing certain objects (e.g., people or cards) arranged on a plain', with each object crossed out or underlined after 'a certain action' -- offered as 'just a thought', not established
constraints.author: allegedly written by David Rayburn, who killed his wife, his step-son, and then himself; found by Linda Rayburn's daughter Jenn, who provided it to Schmeh via a Schneier's-blog connection
constraints.provenance_caveat: 'there's no guarantee that this encrypted note was really written by the late murderer David Rayburn' -- Schmeh flags authorship itself as unconfirmed, independent of any forgery question
constraints.prior_discussion: extensively discussed on Bruce Schneier's blog (2006, schneier.com/blog/archives/2006/01/handwritten_rea.html) and Schmeh's own earlier German-language post (Dec 2013); no plausible solution reported by either

cheap_tests_in_order: 1. Fetch Rayburn-Cryptogram.jpg (scienceblogs.de) and transcribe blind, recording each symbol's identity, position, and underline/strikethrough state separately (the two-state marking is likely to matter more than symbol identity if the diagram hypothesis holds). Cost $1-2, Sonnet.

2. Once transcribed, test the diagram hypothesis directly before any cryptanalysis: does the spatial layout (rows/columns/clusters) resemble a card-game tableau, seating chart, or checklist rather than a written line of text -- since Schmeh's frequency-analysis caveat (most symbols appear once) is exactly what a diagram of ~80 distinct labelled objects would look like, and exactly what a frequency-based cipher test would misread as 'no signal'. Cost $1.

3. Only if test 2 does not support the diagram reading: standard homophonic/keyboard-substitution judged against English with a matched control at the same N and K (same solver); expect a weak signal given N~80 and reported near-hapax frequencies (rule 3: match the design). Cost $2-3.
matched_control: English control (same N=74, 200 samples, tools/data en corpus) and uniform-random control (same N=74 K=59, 200 draws) run 25 Sept 2026, see cheap_test_done[0]

cheap_test_done.method: fetched Rayburn-Cryptogram.jpg (scienceblogs.de, 1 request, HTTP 200), blind one-pass transcription recording symbol identity, position and mark state (underline/strikethrough/overline) separately; wrote ciphers/rayburn-2004/{ciphertext.txt,ciphertext.tsv}; computed IC against a matched English control (same N) and a matched uniform-random control (same N and K)
cheap_test_done.result: N=74 tokens (58 main grid + 8 left-margin + 8 right-margin), K=59 distinct type ids; target IC 0.0056 vs English control mean 0.0618 [0.0311,0.0911] vs uniform-random control mean 0.0171 [0.0115,0.0255] (expected ~1/K=0.0169) -- target below both control ranges, consistent with Schmeh's near-hapax observation and either a high-homophone cipher or non-linguistic content; rules out plain monoalphabetic substitution on frequency grounds, does not decide between the diagram hypothesis and a homophonic cipher
cheap_test_done.cost: see LANE B3 ledger (orchestrator reads get_session, not self-reported)

judge.note: letters_min/max is a rough guess (Schmeh: 'about 80 characters', mixed letters and other keyboard symbols, exact letter-only count unknown pending transcription); PASS/FAIL here is meaningful only if test 2 rules against the diagram hypothesis -- a language judge on a non-linguistic diagram is not a fair test regardless of the result (CLAUDE.md rule 3: match the design)

value: low-medium: an unusually well-specified structural alternative (Schmeh's own diagram hypothesis) that most cryptanalytic write-ups of this item skip past straight to substitution-cipher framing; testing the diagram reading first is cheap and could reclassify the whole target before any letter-frequency work is wasted on it
status_25_Sept_2026: open; plausibly a password/directory list (Bourdeau, Schneier's readers) per UNSOLVED-SURVEY.md row 23 -- consistent with, but distinct from, Schmeh's own diagram hypothesis found in this pass's full read of the post
schema_note: cheap_tests_in_order are proposals (rule 10: an approach is not a claim); a test actually run goes under cheap_test_done with its control. judge block assumes English running text for now (language_candidates lists this as uncertain); if test 2 supports the diagram hypothesis, the right spec change is to drop the letters/language checks entirely and add a structural (layout-clustering) judge instead -- not built here (scope of this brief).
